reading.title: The Summer the Weather Changed
reading.subtitle: A report on three linked natural disasters

paragraphs.label: A.
paragraphs.text: In the summer of 2023, three separate natural disasters struck the same coastal region in the space of six weeks. First came a heat wave: temperatures rose above 42°C for ten consecutive days. Then, when the rains finally arrived, they came with unusual force. Rivers overflowed, and floods swept through several towns. Later that same summer, a wildfire broke out in the hills above the coast, destroying more than 400 hectares of forest. Scientists later described the events as “connected”.

paragraphs.label: B.
paragraphs.text: The heat wave was the first warning. Meteorologists had forecast high temperatures, but few people had expected a heat wave of this intensity. Hospitals reported a sharp rise in admissions for heat exhaustion and dehydration. Local authorities opened cooling centres in public libraries and community halls, where residents could escape the worst of the heat. The heat also dried out the soil and vegetation, creating the perfect conditions for the disasters that followed.

paragraphs.label: C.
paragraphs.text: When the rain came, it was heavy and sudden. Within two days, more than 200 millimetres of rain had fallen — more than the region normally receives in an entire month. Rivers that had been almost dry overflowed their banks. The town of Marlowe was the worst affected: water reached the ground floor of buildings and cut off the main road for nearly a week. Rescue teams used boats to reach residents who had been trapped in their homes. The floods were later described as the worst the region had seen in fifty years.

paragraphs.label: D.
paragraphs.text: The wildfire began in August, three weeks after the floods. By then, the vegetation that had survived the rain had dried out again under the summer sun. Strong winds helped the fire spread quickly across the hills. Firefighters worked for eleven days to bring it under control. Over 400 hectares of forest were destroyed, and several families lost their homes. Although no lives were lost, the ecological damage was severe: many species of plants and small animals were affected, and the soil in the burned areas will take years to recover.

paragraphs.label: E.
paragraphs.text: Scientists who studied the events concluded that they were not separate. The heat wave had dried the vegetation, making the wildfire more likely. The heavy rain that ended the heat wave had been intensified by the unusually warm air, which holds more moisture. The floods, in turn, had washed away trees and weakened riverbanks, making some areas more vulnerable. In other words, each disaster had helped to create the conditions for the next one.

paragraphs.label: F.
paragraphs.text: The events of that summer have prompted local authorities to rethink their emergency planning. New early-warning systems are being installed in coastal towns. Cooling centres will now open automatically when temperatures exceed 38°C. Firebreaks are being widened in the hills, and residents are being trained in evacuation procedures. Scientists warn that similar events will become more common in the future — not because the region is unlucky, but because a warming climate is making extreme weather more frequent and more intense.
